all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: computer
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a computer or processing device is used in a broad sense to mean a device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: interaction design
concepts.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

defining_facts.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: extended reality system
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

concepts.name: software development lifecycle
concepts.definition: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

defining_facts.text: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

A software development lifecycle is a systematic, structured set of connected stages for developing and deploying software that comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities needed to build the software.
Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages.

A software development life cycle (SDLC) is a systematic approach that helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability, because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone.
A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence.

A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage.

The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.

concepts.name: immersive environment
concepts.definition: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience.

defining_facts.text: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience.
Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

concepts.name: user feedback
concepts.definition: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

defining_facts.text: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

concepts.name: requirement gathering
concepts.definition: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

defining_facts.text: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

concepts.name: design-prototype-evaluate cycle
concepts.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.
In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the term design refers only to interface and interaction design, not code design.

A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.

The interface design part of interactive system development uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping, and quick evaluation of the prototype; design may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, quick evaluation may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the cycle is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable; usability testing or an empirical study is therefore needed to estimate usability, although usability was expected because the design-prototype-evaluate cycle was followed.

In the traditional interactive system development lifecycle, the requirement gathering stage may span months; the design-prototype-evaluate stage can take months, although each cycle may take one or two days and, considering repeated cycles and other activities, may take from a couple of weeks to a month; code design may take months or at least a couple of weeks; code testing may take weeks; and an empirical study may take weeks.

concepts.name: design
concepts.definition: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

defining_facts.text: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

concepts.name: code design
concepts.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

defining_facts.text: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

concepts.name: code testing
concepts.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

defining_facts.text: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

concepts.name: interface design
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

concepts.name: testing
concepts.definition: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

defining_facts.text: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

never_defined.name: virtual environment

never_defined.name: computer screen
never_defined.definition: Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) can be a three-dimensional virtual environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, a VR box, or a VR headset, with a VR headset being the common example; users typically have no real physical movements, and examples include virtual tours using only a headset, which can be device-based or web-based.

never_defined.name: screen
never_defined.definition: Augmented reality (AR) customer-experience applications that let a customer preview a product before purchase include the IKEA Place app, which lets a user scan a room and place IKEA objects in the digital image of the room to see how the room would look, and a Dulux visualizer app, which lets a customer digitally paint walls on a screen and see the effect before deciding whether to buy the paint.

never_defined.name: user action

never_defined.name: microphone
never_defined.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

never_defined.name: speaker
never_defined.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

never_defined.name: feature

never_defined.name: interface

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

never_defined.name: task

never_defined.name: software development

never_defined.definition: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation in interactive system development are standard software development lifecycle (SDLC) stages with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality system design or implementation.

never_defined.name: experience design
never_defined.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

never_defined.name: cost overrun
never_defined.definition: A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

never_defined.name: prototyping techniques
never_defined.definition: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

never_defined.name: final product
never_defined.definition: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

never_defined.name: functionality
never_defined.definition: A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.

never_defined.name: system
never_defined.definition: A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.

never_defined.name: horizontal prototyping
never_defined.definition: Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.

never_defined.name: computer program
never_defined.definition: A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

never_defined.name: programmer
never_defined.definition: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

never_defined.name: programming expertise
never_defined.definition: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

never_defined.name: static interface sketch
never_defined.definition: In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

never_defined.definition: International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available.
